descriptions.value: Following his re-election in 1936, Franklin D. Roosevelt began a second presidential term on 20 January 1937, with John Nance Garner as vice-president. His first inauguration had taken place on 4 March 1933; the Twentieth Amendment changed the inauguration date for 1937 onward. Roosevelt communicated with the public through informal radio addresses. Early broadcasts discussed the banking crisis, the New Deal programme and economic recovery, followed by an address on public works and Social Security in 1935. His Good Neighbor Policy sought improved relations and trade with Latin America through a stated commitment to respect and non-intervention. The population figure shown separately is an earlier, geographically limited census observation, not a current-year estimate.
Roosevelt entered his third presidential term in January 1941. American aid to the Allies preceded direct entry into the war. This interval ends with U.S. belligerency in December.

The United States entered the war in late 1941 and coordinated with Britain and the Soviet Union. Cooperation against Nazi Germany included disagreements over the second front. Roosevelt’s death in April 1945 brought Truman to the presidency.

Truman took office after Roosevelt’s death in April 1945. His presidential calendar documents the administration through January 1953. The end of the Second World War did not produce a new United States map identity: the presidency and bicameral Congress remained institutions of the same federal constitutional state. This profile covers the administration without attaching later presidents to earlier selected years.

Eisenhower’s presidency began on 20 January 1953. His administration occupied a Cold War setting, while domestic measures included the interstate highway programme. The presidential library’s chronology records both domestic legislation and international diplomacy, including the 1959 opening of the St. Lawrence Seaway with Queen Elizabeth II. The earlier census observation remains labelled with its original date and territorial scope.

descriptions.value: George VI became king after Edward VIII’s abdication in December 1936. Chamberlain’s Conservative premiership began in May 1937. British policy sought to avoid another European war through negotiation and concessions; the Munich agreement of 1938 became its best-known expression. The monarch and prime minister held distinct offices within a parliamentary monarchy. The British Empire extended well beyond the United Kingdom’s domestic population series. This interval ends when Britain entered the war in September 1939.

Britain entered war against Germany in September 1939 while Chamberlain remained prime minister. The outbreak of war changed the setting of government and foreign policy, but did not merge the monarchy and premiership into a single office. Chamberlain resigned on 10 May 1940; George VI then asked Churchill to form a government. This overview ends at that governmental transition.

Churchill became prime minister in May 1940 and formed a wartime coalition. His Conservative affiliation should not be mistaken for the composition of that all-party administration. Britain’s war effort depended on military operations and cooperation with allies; the government continued to operate through parliamentary institutions. George VI remained monarch throughout the war. The leadership records preserve the change to Attlee in 1945 rather than assigning one prime minister to the entire transition year.

Attlee’s Labour government followed the 1945 election. Its programme expanded public services and nationalised important industries. The National Health Service and national insurance legislation were central to postwar reconstruction. Overseas, the government presided over independence for India and Pakistan and the end of British rule in other territories. These were changes in imperial relationships, not grounds for treating every formerly governed territory as a part of the United Kingdom’s domestic census population.

Churchill returned to the premiership in 1951, with Anthony Eden and then Harold Macmillan following during the decade. Elizabeth II succeeded George VI in February 1952. Under Macmillan, the Conservatives increased their majority in the 1959 election. Britain’s international position involved Cold War diplomacy and changing imperial relationships. The domestic population estimate is separately dated and does not include the populations of overseas possessions.

The Acts of Union joined Great Britain and Ireland in 1801, replacing the separate Irish Parliament with representation at Westminster. Constitutional union did not immediately eliminate the separate Irish monetary unit; assimilation with sterling was completed in 1826.

The Irish Free State was established in December 1922; Northern Ireland remained in the United Kingdom. The change in territory preceded the 1927 title legislation. Earlier British-and-Irish source names must not be mistaken for the borders or political identity of the independent Irish state.

descriptions.value: After Hitler’s appointment as chancellor in January 1933, the Nazi leadership dismantled Germany’s democratic institutions and suppressed political opposition. The regime used emergency powers and legislation to concentrate authority, while excluding opponents from public life. Following President Hindenburg’s death in August 1934, Hitler combined presidential authority with the chancellorship. The Nazi Party dominated a dictatorship rather than a competitive parliamentary system. This overview describes the consolidated regime of the mid-1930s, without treating its later territorial conquests as facts about every selected year. The atlas’s boundary reconstructions are a separate geographical source and do not establish the constitutional or political status of every territory represented on the map.

Germany’s invasion of Poland in September 1939 began the European phase of the Second World War. Britain and France declared war in response. The Nazi dictatorship remained in place while German military campaigns expanded into other countries. Wartime territorial control and occupation should not be treated as proof that all conquered populations formed an unchanged national census unit. The German population figures in this dossier retain the territorial definitions of their statistical source.

Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, widening the war in Europe. Nazi rule combined dictatorship and persecution with military occupation across extensive territories. The conflict imposed destruction on occupied societies and on Germany itself. The profile’s leadership coverage ends with Hitler’s death in April 1945. The atlas’s later occupation-zone identities remain separate: no modern German state or occupation authority is silently inserted as the same Nazi-period political identity.

descriptions.value: The Soviet Union was governed through a Communist Party dictatorship. By the mid-1930s, Joseph Stalin had eliminated major rivals and consolidated control over party and state. Forced collectivisation and centrally directed industrial development had imposed severe costs on the population. Political policing and repression were central instruments of government. During 1936–1938, public trials and mass persecution formed part of the Great Terror, which reached its height in 1937–1938. Leadership here refers to Stalin’s dominant position in the party-state system, rather than an assumed presidential or prime-ministerial office. The constitutional description and the practice of party dictatorship are kept distinct.

The Soviet Union concluded a non-aggression pact with Nazi Germany in August 1939, then occupied eastern Poland and fought Finland. Relations with the United States deteriorated without diplomatic recognition being withdrawn. Germany’s invasion in June 1941 ended this political setting.

Germany’s invasion in June 1941 changed the Soviet Union’s position. Cooperation with Britain and the United States developed into a wartime alliance, despite disagreements over strategy. Soviet losses were devastating. The earlier census figure cannot represent wartime population or casualties.

The wartime alliance unravelled after the conflict. Stalin remained dominant until his death in March 1953. Communist Party control continued alongside the formal institutions of the constitutional federation and Supreme Soviet. The later reconsideration of Stalin’s legacy belongs to a separate overview period.

Stalin’s death in 1953 opened a struggle among leading Soviet officials. Khrushchev consolidated his position by the middle of the decade. At the Twentieth Party Congress in 1956, he criticised Stalin’s abuses while defending the Communist system. De-Stalinisation and a policy of peaceful coexistence changed the political setting; they did not transform the Soviet Union into the later Russian Federation. Each displayed census observation retains its own date and Union-wide territorial scope.

descriptions.value: The Meiji Constitution placed the emperor at the centre of the constitutional order. Its provisions described imperial sovereignty and provided for legislative power to be exercised with the Imperial Diet. The Diet consisted of a House of Peers and a House of Representatives. Ministers of state advised the emperor and bore responsibility for their advice. This dossier records those constitutional provisions rather than assuming that the formal document explains every aspect of political practice in the 1930s. Its curated coverage is limited to the imperial polity represented by the mapped identity. It does not use the post-war constitution or a modern government profile as a silent substitute for the selected historical period.

The war in China that expanded in 1937 increasingly shaped Japan’s foreign relations. Japanese military operations and territorial ambitions brought escalating tension with the United States, which opposed the expansion of the conflict. At home, the Meiji Constitution continued to define imperial sovereignty and a bicameral Imperial Diet. Prime ministers changed repeatedly in 1939 and 1940; the dated cabinet records preserve those transitions. Prefectural census figures describe a narrower territory than the whole empire.

Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 brought direct war with the United States. The imperial constitutional framework remained distinct from the postwar constitution that later established popular sovereignty and a symbolic imperial office. This dossier’s interval concerns the imperial map identity; it does not substitute an occupation authority or postwar government when that identity is absent from a boundary snapshot.

The Meiji Constitution came into force on 29 November 1890. It vested sovereignty in the emperor and provided for ministers and a Diet consisting of Peers and Representatives. Formal constitutional provisions are distinguished from political practice.

descriptions.value: The constitution effective from May 1947 established popular sovereignty. The emperor became a symbol of the state, while the Diet consisted of the House of Representatives and House of Councillors. The cabinet exercised executive authority and was collectively responsible to the Diet. Hirohito continued in the imperial office, but its constitutional meaning differed from the Meiji framework. Prime ministerial changes are shown separately; this continuity of a person is not continuity of the earlier system of imperial sovereignty. These domestic constitutional institutions operated during the Allied occupation, under the authority of the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers.

The peace treaty took effect on 28 April 1952, ending the Allied occupation and restoring Japan to sovereign equality. The 1947 constitution continued to place sovereignty in the people, with an emperor who symbolised the state, a bicameral Diet and a cabinet responsible to it. This post-occupation setting differs both from the earlier imperial framework and from the first years of the new constitution under occupation. Changes of prime minister are recorded separately.

descriptions.value: The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred the East India Company’s administrative powers, possessions and armed forces to the British Crown. Responsibility in Britain passed to a Secretary of State for India, while the Crown appointed the viceroy and governors. Later constitutional reforms changed the institutions within this imperial framework. This arrangement is commonly described as the British Raj. It was an imperial system, rather than an independent national government. The mapped entity should not be read as proof of uniform direct British administration across all of the subcontinent. Princely states had a distinct position, and the geographical dataset’s authority fields provide only a simplified representation. This dossier keeps that distinction visible rather than treating administrative control as an unqualified statement of sovereignty.

The viceroy declared India a belligerent in the Second World War in 1939 without consulting the elected provincial representatives. The Indian National Congress intensified its campaign for independence. British imperial administration therefore faced both the demands of war and opposition to continued colonial rule. New Delhi was the administrative capital. The broader Indian census totals shown separately exclude Burma and should not be read as the population of a single directly administered map polygon. The later partition into India and Pakistan is recorded as a dated transition, not inferred from overlap between map snapshots.

The 1875 constitutional laws established a republican parliamentary framework with two chambers and ministers responsible to them. Parliament moved back from Versailles to Paris in 1879. Presidents and parliamentary institutions are distinct from the rapidly changing ministries.

Defeat and occupation in 1940 produced competing claims to French authority. Pétain’s constitutional acts adjourned the parliamentary chambers, while de Gaulle led Free France. In August 1944 the provisional authorities asserted that republican legality had continued and repudiated the Vichy constitutional acts.

The provisional government restored republican authority, with de Gaulle heading the September 1944 government until January 1946. The later Fourth and Fifth republics had different constitutional frameworks. Presidential terms are retained separately, including Auriol, Coty and de Gaulle; detailed ministry and transition gaps remain unfilled.
